To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
circulating tumor cells, exosomes, and extracellular nucleics acids are present in blood, plasma, serum of breast cancer patients, and may be used as biomarkers for early cancer detection.
circulating tumor cells, nucleic acids, including extracellular mRNPs, are detectable in breast cancer patients.
extracellular RNAs are present in the circulation of cancer patients, and their detection may be used to monitor the disease.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel methods for the diagnosis of cancer and the monitoring of disease progression.
the identification of novel biomarkers that are present in blood, plasma, serum and exosomes of patients with breast cancer.

the identification of circulating tumor cells and extrosomal nucleic acids, particularly mRNAs, in blood and other bodily fluids as a means for early cancer diagnosis and prognosis, and for the identification of potential therapeutic targets.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the presence of circulating tumor cells in the blood of breast cancer patients is a strong prognostic marker for metastatic disease.

the detection of circulating tumor cells is a promising method to improve the diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment of breast cancer patients, but the current evidence does not yet allow the use of circulating tumor cells as a routine diagnostic tool.
there is no conclusive evidence that circulating tumor cells and/or extracellular nucleic acid biomarkers are clinically relevant in the detection and/or prognosis of breast cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the detection of circulating tumor cells and extranuclear nucleic acids, especially exosomes, may be a useful tool in the diagnosis and prognosis for breast cancer, but that further research is required to establish a clinically applicable test.
circulating tumor cells and extranuclear nucleic acids, particularly exosomes, are clinically relevant biomarkers for breast cancer.

the detection of circulating nucleic acids in the blood, serum or plasma of patients with cancer is a promising approach in the diagnosis and prognosis for breast cancer, but that the detection of such nucleic acids alone may not provide sufficient specificity to warrant their clinical utility in isolation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
circulating tumor cells and extraviolet nucleic acids, especially extracellular mRNPs, are promising biomarkers for early diagnosis and prognosis of cancer.

the presence of extracellular RNAs in blood, plasma, or serum of breast cancer patients is indicative of tumor progression and metastases, and that the presence of such extracellular nucleic acid species in the peripheral circulation of cancer patients is a promising biomarker for the diagnosis and prognosis, as well as the tailoring of treatment for breast cancer.
the detection of extracellular nucleic acid molecules in the peripheral blood of patients is feasible and may be used to detect the presence and/or progression of cancer in the future.
